# Getting in without credentials

You have a repository with a notebook in it. It runs top to bottom from a clean
start, and the README says where the data came from. Chapter 26 got you that
far. Here's the question Chapter 26 didn't answer: who opens it? A public
repository doesn't make anybody look at it, and there's nobody standing next to
you to hand it to.

## Which doors need the degree

Say this once, then move past it. A posting that says PhD required means PhD
required. It isn't an opening bid, and no amount of good work argues past it.
Same for a program whose eligibility section says currently enrolled. If you've
already graduated, that door shut on the day you did, and being better at the
work doesn't reopen it.

So read the eligibility line before the description. It sits near the bottom,
and it's the only sentence that decides whether the rest of the page is about
you. An evening spent on an application you were never eligible for is one of
the three hours you had this week.

Everything else in this chapter is a door where nobody checks.

## The smallest contribution that counts

Open-source projects take work from strangers by design. There's no
application, and nothing in the process asks who you work for. Most people
picture that work as code, go hunting for a bug they could fix, find they can't
read the codebase yet, and stop.

Start at the other end. File issues, and fix documentation.

A public repository carries a tab beside its files holding that project's
[issues]{.term def="One numbered public thread on a project's tracker, where
somebody reports a problem and the maintainers answer."}. Anybody with a free
account can open one, and nobody assigns them. Go and find that tab on the
repository you published in Chapter 26. Yours is empty. Then find the same tab
on a project you used in this book and read the five most recent.

Here's why filing one is a real contribution rather than a consolation prize.
What a maintainer is short of is reproductions: sets of steps somebody else can
run that make the broken thing break again.

Code from a stranger arrives as a question. Somebody has to decide whether it's
correct and whether it breaks something they can't see from where they sit. An
issue that reproduces arrives as an answer, and reading it is the whole cost.

Documentation works the same way, and it's the easier of the two to start on.
Whoever wrote that page knows what it meant and can't see the gap any more. You
hit the gap this month, so for a few weeks you're the only one who can point at
it. Pointing at it in an issue counts. Nobody is waiting for you to write the
replacement page.

The first move is small and specific. Go back to the place in this book where a
tool's own documentation made you stop and guess. Chapter 17 is the likeliest
one, because it's the only chapter that hands you somebody else's library.
Library documentation gets written for people who already know what the library
is for. Now write down four things.

``` {.default}
Version:  the exact version string the tool printed for you
Steps:    what you ran, in the order you ran it
Expected: what the documentation led you to expect
Actual:   what came back, pasted, not described
```

Three of those four came out of Chapter 16 under other names. What you were
trying to get is Expected, the cut-down code is Steps, the verbatim error is
Actual.

The version is the one that's new. A forum answers a question about your code.
An issue makes a claim about somebody else's, and they'll want to know which
build you were on.

The last label is where people go wrong. Paste what came back. Don't tidy it,
don't summarize it, don't retype it from memory. A maintainer searches their own
code for the string you paste, and a paraphrase matches nothing.

Plenty of issues get no reply at all. That isn't a verdict on you, and it isn't
information either.

## Writing to somebody whose paper you read

The standard advice here is to network, and networking happens between people
who are already in the same room. You aren't in the room. Here's the version
you can act on tonight: one message, to one person, about one thing you already
did.

The order in that sentence is the trick. You have a repository from Chapter 26
with a figure in it that somebody else published first. That's why this chapter
comes after that one. Without it you're writing a request. With it you're
writing a result and a question, and the two get read differently.

``` {.default}
Subject: reproduced Figure 2 of <short paper reference> from GEO

Dear Dr <surname>,

I reproduced Figure 2 of <short paper reference> from <accession>.
The notebook runs top to bottom from a clean start: <link>.

My version separates the two cell types in the same order yours
does. The one thing I could not work out is <one question, one
sentence>.

I am not asking for a position or for your time beyond a sentence.
If there is a short answer I would be glad to have it, and if
there is not, no reply is needed.

<your name>
<link to the rest of your work>
```

Now the annotations. The template is disposable. The reasons aren't.

Your subject line names their work and what you did to it. I've sent the other
kind, the one that reads `Inquiry regarding research opportunities`, and it
tells the reader nothing about whether the next thirty seconds are worth
spending.

Lead with a thing you did. Not your background, not your interest in the field.
Those are claims, and a stranger has no way to check a claim.

That's also why the link sits in the opening paragraph. It's the only part they
can verify without taking your word for anything. Put it at the bottom and only
the people who read to the bottom see it.

Keep the question narrow enough to answer in one line. A question like `Do you
have any advice?` can't be answered at all, which is why it isn't. `Did you
filter the low-count genes before or after normalizing?` can be answered while
somebody's standing up.

The line that looks cuttable is the one saying what you aren't asking for, and
it's what makes the message cheap to answer. A message that might be building
toward a request for a position costs the reader a decision first. This one
costs a sentence, or nothing.

Keep it shorter than their screen, and write to the person whose paper you
actually used rather than to the head of the department.

Now the outcome, honestly. I have no measured response rate to give you and I
won't invent one. Most of these produce nothing. Treat silence as the ordinary
result and read nothing into it. You can't tell a message that was read and
declined from one that was never opened, and neither can anybody else.

A few produce two lines, and once in a while one produces an exchange that runs
for a month. So send them on a schedule rather than judging them one at a time:
one a week, to people whose papers you were reading anyway.

<!-- nlr-allow: 404 -->

::: {.trap}
Click the link in your own message. It opens, because you're signed in to the
account that owns it. A private repository and a Drive file set to restricted
both look exactly like public ones to their owner. The person you wrote to gets
a sign-in wall or a 404, decides the link is broken, and doesn't reply to tell
you so.
:::

## Which programs will take you

A program a university department runs for its own undergraduates is closed to
you, and so is any summer scheme wanting a supervisor's letter or a current
transcript. The one you'll get pointed at anyway is the NSF's Research
Experiences for Undergraduates. Its own solicitation says students who have
received their bachelor's degrees and are no longer enrolled as undergraduates
are generally not eligible. Funded places also go only to US citizens, US
nationals and permanent residents. Go and see that for yourself, before
somebody who never read it tells you to apply.

Google Summer of Code runs the other way. It pays people to work on an
open-source project for a few months, and it doesn't ask you to be enrolled
anywhere. Its eligibility page gets the same treatment as the NSF's, and three
things are on it. You have to be 18 or over, you have to be allowed to
work where you live, and it wants people who are new to open source.

Filing issues doesn't cost you that last one. Landing a steady stream of
patches eventually will, which is a nice problem to have.

Your application there is a written proposal to one project from a published
list. Mentors at that project pick the proposals, and they can see who's been
filing issues on it, which is why the previous section comes first.

A competition never asks the question at all. A leaderboard is a number, and a
number doesn't care where you work. A Kaggle account costs nothing
and a public rank is a link you can send. Its rules do exclude residents of a
handful of sanctioned countries, so read the eligibility line on the competition
rather than here. Chapter 27 has the reason not to spend every week this way.

The slowest route is the one that accumulates. Chapter 16 sent you to Biostars
with a question. It takes an answer from anybody too, and what sits beside your
answer there is a vote count rather than a job title. Go and check that on a
thread before you believe me. Answer one question a week that you can genuinely
answer, and after a year that's a public record a stranger can search.

::: {.asof}
The NSF and Google Summer of Code eligibility pages were read on 2 August 2026.
Both get rewritten. What doesn't move is the shape: one section, usually near
the bottom, saying who may apply. Read it on the program's own page before you
spend an evening on the form.
:::

## What a portfolio has to do

An affiliation answers one question before a stranger asks it: has anybody
watched this person work? You can't produce that answer. You can produce the
work itself, in a form somebody can check without asking you for anything.

First, it opens. One link, no account, no request-access button. The notebook
renders with its output under every cell, so a reader who won't start a runtime
can still see what came back.

Second, it explains itself with you out of the room. The README answers the four
questions Chapter 26 gave it. The one people drop is the accession, and a number
nobody can trace back to a file is a number nobody can check.

Third, it says what it didn't establish. Chapters 26 and 27 both had you write
that sentence down. Put it in the README rather than waiting to be asked for
it. Anybody can post a plot. A stated limit is the part that reads like
somebody who's done this before.

::: {.check}
Open a private browsing window, sign in to nothing, and paste your own
repository link into it. You should get the README, and clicking through to the
notebook should show output underneath the cells. A sign-in wall, a 404, or a
notebook with empty output areas each mean the same thing: nobody but you has
ever seen this.
:::

## Exercises

::: {.exercise num="28.1" time="45 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Write an issue for a real gap you hit in this book, in a form somebody who has
never met you can act on.
:::
::: {.given}
The tool, the exact version string it printed for you, and the page or notebook
cell where you stopped and guessed. If none comes to mind, start at Chapter 17,
for the reason above.
:::
::: {.produce}
Four labeled parts under 200 words: version, steps, expected, actual. The actual
output is pasted, not described. Add the address of the issue you filed, if the
gap is real and still there.
:::
::: {.check}
Start a fresh Colab runtime and follow your own steps exactly as written, adding
nothing. The problem should happen again. If it doesn't, what you have isn't a
reproduction yet, and the missing piece is usually a step you'd done so often
you stopped seeing it.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="6"}
:::
:::

::: {.exercise num="28.2" time="30 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Draft the message about your Chapter 26 project, addressed to the person whose
figure you reproduced.
:::
::: {.given}
The repository link you wrote into Exercise 26.1, and one technical question
about their methods that you genuinely could not answer from the paper.
:::
::: {.produce}
One message under 150 words carrying five things: what you did, a link, one
question, one sentence saying what you aren't asking for, and your name.
:::
::: {.check}
Work out the shortest honest answer to your question. If it runs past two
sentences, the question is too big and a busy person won't start it. Then paste
your link into a logged-out window. Sending the message is your call, and the
artifact this exercise wants is the message.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="6"}
:::
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="You sent eight messages and nobody replied to any of them"}
That's the ordinary outcome and it says nothing about your work. Check two
things before changing anything. Open your own link in a logged-out window.
Read your first sentence and ask whether it describes something you did or
something you want. After that, keep the cadence and change the recipients.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Your issue was closed with one line and no discussion"}
Read what the line says. Answered means the question had a short answer, which
is a normal result. Cannot reproduce means your steps weren't enough on somebody
else's machine, and the fix is the version string plus the exact input. Reopen
it only when you have something new to add.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The eligibility page says you must be currently enrolled"}
Then that door is shut, and it stays shut however good the application would
have been. Close the tab. Spend the evening on an open-source issue or on
Exercise 28.2, neither of which has an eligibility section.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Somebody replied asking what it is you want"}
Your message didn't say what it wasn't asking for, so they've had to ask.
Answer in one sentence, then put that sentence into the template for next time.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Find the eligibility line on a program page and say in one word whether it
  includes you
- File an issue carrying a version string, steps, expected and actual, with the
  actual output pasted rather than described
- Name the one thing a cold message has to contain before its first paragraph
  ends
- Open your own repository in a logged-out window and say what a stranger sees
- State one thing your reproduced figure establishes and one thing it doesn't
:::
